The chapters follow LESSON['lecture'] in order (three spheres; the Moon's month; always a ball; round and round; what people used to think), in the lesson's own words and with the lesson's own drawings: ART.scene globe and sky for the Earth and the Sun, ART.sim moonPhases for the month, the lamp-and-ball model of the demo step, ART.kit.earthMoonSvg for the model the child builds, and the four pictures of the lesson's history step.
title: The Moon
subtitle: Grade 3 Science
objectives: Describe the regular change in the position and appearance of the Moon.
Describe the relative movement of the Earth and Moon.
Describe the Earth, Sun and Moon as approximately spherical.
Talk about how some of the scientific knowledge and thinking now was different in the past.

beats.say: Look up at the Moon tonight, and again next week. It will look different.
It is the same ball of rock all month, going round the Earth.
The Earth, the Sun and the Moon are all shaped like balls.
A ball shape is called a sphere. So all three are spheres.
The Sun is a huge ball of hot, glowing gas. Never look straight at it.
The Earth looks flat from where you stand, because it is so big.
From space it is a round blue ball, not a flat plate.
Look at the Moon night after night, and it seems to change.
It starts as a new Moon. The side facing us is dark.
Then a thin crescent, then a half Moon, then a full circle.
Growing is called waxing. Shrinking back down is called waning.
The whole pattern takes about four weeks, and then it starts again.
The Moon does not really change shape. It is always a ball.
Make a model with a grown-up: a lamp in a dark room, and a ball on a stick.
The lamp is the Sun. It lights one half of the ball, and the other half stays dark.
Your head is the Earth. Hold the ball up, and turn slowly on the spot.
You see a thin crescent, then a half, then the whole lit face.
The ball never changed shape. Only how much of its lit half you could see.

at.much: how much of its lit half

beats.say: The Moon travels round the Earth. That path is called its orbit.
One trip round takes about four weeks: a month, not a day.
The Earth itself spins on the spot, once every day.
That spin is what gives us day and night, over and over.
Today you will build this model on screen, and make it move.
Long ago, many people thought the Earth was flat, like a plate.
They watched the Sun cross the sky and thought it went round us.
Then telescopes showed the Moon is a rocky ball, with craters.
In 1969 astronauts stood on the Moon and photographed the Earth.
Science changes when people look more carefully.
The Earth, the Sun and the Moon are all spheres: ball shapes.
The phases go new, crescent, half, full, and back to new. It is always a ball.
It goes round the Earth in a month. The Earth spins once a day.
And our ideas change when we look more carefully.
